unresolved.problem: Claims the lightning conductor, 30 m away, 'experienced a large attraction' via Coulomb's law from induced charge and the roof being closest to the cloud; but the exemplar also says the roof is the structure the cloud acted on most strongly, while the tall conductor has smaller r. These two claims are in tension; the explanation also treats the cloud and roof as point charges though Coulomb's law is for point charges and the lessons' explanation of lightning interception through a point-charge force is not valid.

The prompt asks why the roof, not the wooden stall, was acted on most strongly, which presupposes the answer; also the exemplar says the force is 'proportional to 1/r^2' from the graph, whereas F is proportional to 1/r^2 only for the straight-line graph. Minor, but the (a) prompt refers to students' own F vs 1/r^2 graph though it was from a given data set, not an experiment they did (Lesson 3).

Says the cloud affected the charges in the traders' bodies 'so the hairs all gained the same type of charge'. Induction on the body gives charge separation, not net charge gained without contact or earthing; also inconsistent with Part 2 teaching on induction (charge redistributes, sign depends). The hairs repelling needs the hairs to carry the same charge via the body, which is not explained by induction.

Part 4(d) says the lightning conductor releases the stored energy to Earth, while Part 2(c) and Part 5 say it keeps induced charge draining so no discharge builds; the lightning conductor is said both to drain charge gradually and to give the discharge a safe path. Part 5 also says charge builds up in the cloud 'by transfer of electrons' with no mechanism, and the exemplar lists the Coulomb-force step as pulling to ionise air, which is a loose claim.
